vignette:
He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life around danger, first in military service and later as a bomb disposal technician, and he has always described himself as someone who is calm when others panic. For years, that identity fits him. He is the man who counts wires, checks exits, and keeps his voice level when everyone else is raising theirs. At home, he is a husband, a father, and the person his family turns to when something feels uncertain. That sense of control begins to change during the period when his youngest child becomes critically ill.

At first, he tells himself that the hospital stay will be temporary, just another crisis to manage. His child is admitted with a life-threatening condition, and suddenly the routines that usually keep him steady no longer work. He cannot solve this problem with training or procedure. He sits beside the bed watching monitors, listening for the change in tone from nurses and doctors, terrified of the moments when they step out of the room to “check something.” He remembers the smell of disinfectant, the bright fluorescent light, and the way his mind keeps scanning for danger even though the threat is not visible. He finds himself fixating on small details—his child’s breathing, the beeping machines, the movement of staff in the corridor—as if noticing everything can somehow protect his child.

When the illness becomes more severe, he starts to lose time. He moves through the days on autopilot, answering questions and signing forms, but later he cannot remember parts of conversations. He sleeps in short, broken stretches, waking startled and instantly alert, as if hearing a blast or an alarm. Even after the immediate crisis passes, his body does not believe it is over. At home he becomes jumpy at unexpected sounds, especially hospital-like noises such as pagers, monitor alarms, or even the ping of a phone. He flinches more than he wants anyone to see, and he is embarrassed by how quickly his heart races.

After his child survives, family and friends speak of gratitude and relief, but he feels something more complicated and harder to name. He is relieved, yes, yet he is also haunted by how close he came to losing a child. He begins to replay the worst moments without wanting to. Certain images return uninvited: his child’s still face under the hospital lights, a doctor’s serious expression, the endless wait outside the ICU. These memories arrive not as stories but as sensations, pulling him back into the fear as if it is happening again. He tries to push them away by keeping busy, returning to work, and focusing on tasks that require precision. His job offers a kind of familiar structure, and for a while he leans into it, staying late, double-checking equipment, and taking on extra calls because being occupied feels safer than being alone with his thoughts.

Even so, the hypervigilance follows him. He notices it in ordinary places: at home, he scans the room before sitting down; in public, he chooses seats near exits; at work, he is already alert, though the danger there feels more manageable than the helplessness he felt in the hospital. He becomes more irritable with his wife and quieter with his children, then feels guilty for both. He wants to be present, but part of him remains on watch, waiting for something else to go wrong. He finds it harder to relax, harder to sleep, and harder to stop his mind once it starts turning over what-ifs. He avoids talking about the hospitalization because even brief conversations bring back the panic and the helplessness he worked so hard not to feel at the time.

Over the months, he realizes that the hospital experience has changed how he moves through the world. He still functions, still works, still provides for his family, but it takes more effort than before, and he feels exhausted by the effort of keeping himself together. What finally brings him to seek help is a night when he wakes from a vivid nightmare about his child dying in the hospital and cannot calm his breathing. He sits at the edge of the bed, shaken and sweating, aware that he can no longer keep pretending the fear has passed on its own.
